title: Parliament recalled from 30 November as Centre makes second attempt at delimitation bill
dek: The Lok Sabha meets on Monday and the Rajya Sabha on Wednesday for 'essential government business', expected to be the bill to enlarge the Lok Sabha to as many as 850 seats and bring in women's reservation. The Opposition says it will resist.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Parliament will sit again from Monday, 30 November, after the Union government asked the presiding officers to recall both Houses at four days' notice for what it called "essential government business", setting up a second attempt to pass the constitutional amendment that would enlarge the Lok Sabha through delimitation and bring in reservation for women. The same amendment fell short of a two-thirds majority in April.

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has directed that the House, adjourned sine die on 13 August, will meet at 11 am on Monday, and Rajya Sabha Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan has called the Upper House for 11 am on Wednesday, 2 December, according to the public broadcaster's report of the Lok Sabha bulletin. Both Houses may finish on 3 December. There will be no Question Hour, Zero Hour or Private Members' Business. The government has not published its agenda, but it is widely expected to bring back the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, according to reports. The Opposition says the sitting is about delimitation, not women's representation, and has said it will fight the bill.

## What happened

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced on Thursday, Constitution Day, that the government had asked the Speaker and the Chairman to reconvene the Houses. Because the Monsoon Session was adjourned on 13 August but never prorogued, the formal step that ends a session, the new sittings are legally a continuation of it rather than a new Winter Session. The Speaker can call such a sitting under Rule 15 of the Lok Sabha's rules, according to reports.

The Union Cabinet was expected to take up the legislative proposals on Friday, according to reports citing unnamed officials. No bill text had been circulated to members by Friday afternoon.

The package defeated in April would raise the Lok Sabha's maximum strength from 543 to as many as 850 seats, redraw constituencies through a Delimitation Commission that could start work before the next Census is complete, and bring in one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies in time for the 2029 general election. The government is considering raising every state's seats by about 50% to answer fears that southern states would lose relative weight, according to reports.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in a signed article published on Thursday, said the April defeat "should fill our hearts with shame" and wrote: "I assure the 'Nari Shakti' of India that no force can prevent us from ensuring that justice is done to them."

## The numbers

A constitutional amendment needs a majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting. With every seat filled and every member voting, that is 362 in the 543-member Lok Sabha; reports put the figure at about 361 because of vacancies. On 17 April, 298 members voted for the amendment and 230 against; of 528 votes cast, the government needed 352, according to reports. After that defeat it withdrew the Delimitation Bill, 2026, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026.

- About 320: NDA strength in the Lok Sabha, according to reports
- 22: DMK members, who have not announced support
- 8: NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar) members, also uncommitted
- 4: YSR Congress Party members, described in reports as potentially decisive

The DMK wants the freeze on seat allocation based on the 1971 Census extended by 25 years, with safeguards written into the bill, according to reports. The Samajwadi Party has signalled that it will oppose the bill once it is tabled, according to reports. A BJP leader said the government was "keen and determined" to get the bill passed and has assured some non-ruling parties that delimitation will be fair, according to reports.

## What the Opposition says

Jairam Ramesh, the Congress general secretary in charge of communications, said on Friday in a post on X that the government was "lying" about the purpose of the sitting. Women's reservation is already law, he said: the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam was passed unanimously in September 2023 but notified only at 10.40 pm on 16 April 2026. He called the recall "a desperate move by a nervous and rattled PM" and said it "will be countered with firm resolve". On Thursday he had asked: "Can there be a greater insult to and assault on the Constitution?"

The Congress has set out three demands: keep the present size of the Lok Sabha for 25 more years, keep the present state-wise distribution of seats for 25 more years, and bring in one-third reservation for women, including sub-quotas for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe women, from the 2029 election. It alleges the government wants a "super-tainted" two-thirds majority built on defections and mergers.

Gaurav Gogoi, the Congress deputy leader in the Lok Sabha, wrote on X: "No question hour, No zero hour, No Private Members bill in Parliament." Congress MP Manish Tewari said the request "mocks the institution of Parliament" and that it was time for the Winter Session to convene. CPI(M) Rajya Sabha member John Brittas said: "A majority manufactured through political manipulation is not a mandate. It is a mockery of democracy." Shashi Tharoor, a Congress MP, called it "a fight to save Indian democracy".

## Background

The 131st Amendment Bill was made public on 14 April, Ambedkar Jayanti, and introduced on 16 April by Arjun Ram Meghwal, Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Law and Justice, days before Assembly elections in West Bengal, Assam and Tamil Nadu. It was defeated at a special sitting on the night of 17 April. Home Minister Amit Shah had told the Lok Sabha during that debate that no state would lose relative strength.

Since then the Monsoon Session ran from 20 July to 13 August, and the government kept it open for more than 100 days without announcing Winter Session dates, which the Congress said last week showed the government was waiting until it was sure of the numbers.

## Why it matters for Bengal

West Bengal has 42 Lok Sabha seats. How the extra seats are shared between states, and whether delimitation uses fresh population figures, will decide whether Bengal's share of the House rises or falls relative to faster-growing northern states. In April, Mamata Banerjee, then chief minister, said her party would support the women's bill but not delimitation, while the BJP said the commission would consult all parties.

## What happens next

- Friday, 27 November: Cabinet expected to consider the proposals, according to reports.
- Monday, 30 November: Lok Sabha meets at 11 am.
- Wednesday, 2 December: Rajya Sabha meets at 11 am.
- Thursday, 3 December: sittings may end, subject to business.

If the amendment passes both Houses, it would also need ratification by at least half of the state legislatures because it affects representation of states in Parliament.
